there is no evidence of a biomechanical deterioration of the segments adjacent to a 1 level cervical fusion.
the kinematics at segments adjacent to an arthrodesis did not change in a significant way 12 months after an operation.
a one-level cervical disc replacement does not change the mobility at adjacent cranial or caudal levels in a clinically significant manner.

the biomechanical changes in the cervical spine after a one-level anterior arthrodesis, and we did not find evidence of increased mobility.

the present study did not provide evidence of increased segmental motion after a one-level arthrodesis of the cervical spine.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have not seen any evidence of accelerated degeneration of adjacent segments in our study.
the cervical spine is not an ideal candidate for a motion preservation implant.
the biomechanical situation in the adjacent segments is not altered by the one-level cervical fusion procedure.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a one-level cervical spine fusion is a safe and reliable procedure.
the development of symptomatic adjacent segment disease after a one-level anterior cervical fusion is not due to a biomechanical effect of fusion.
the development of adjacent segment degeneration is a multifactorial process, and that a one-level arthrodesis does not seem to be a major risk factor.
